title: What Happens When Your Nose Runs in the Cold?
description:
Send this to the friend who always needs a tissue the second they step outside.
In one study of 90 people at a ski-resort clinic, 96% who were out in the cold had some runny nose (Northwestern Medicine). Your nose warms and wets every breath before it reaches your lungs (Harvard Health), and cold, dry air trips a nerve reflex, the same kind of system that makes your mouth water before a meal, so your glands pour out extra mucus (Smithsonian, Cleveland Clinic). When you breathe out, warm wet air hits the cooler lining of your nose and condenses, winning back up to a third of the water (Baraniuk, NIH PMC). A runny nose that lasts more than three weeks or comes with a fever is worth seeing a doctor about (Cleveland Clinic).

safety: Curious-friend tone, no personal medical advice, no product or medication advice (Northwestern's OTC list not used). Voiced safety line uses Cleveland Clinic 'lasts more than three weeks or occurs with a fever' -> 'See a doctor'. Dropped or not voiced: the 96 degrees F nasal-air figure (Smithsonian) because NIH reviews give ~30 C (86 F) for posterior nasal air, so the temperature is disputed and kept off screen; the 48.6% skier prevalence (PubMed 11732814) because the abstract could not be loaded to verify; 'below 40 degrees' (Smithsonian phrasing is an example, 'say below 40 degrees', not a threshold); the 'nostrils switch every four hours' fact (off topic). The condensation-joins-the-drip fact (Smithsonian) is visual only, not voiced, to keep length.
